Our statistical reference is Anderson and colleagues' *Essentials of Modern Business Statistics with Microsoft Excel*, 8th edition (2020). We use **R** for analysis and **Quarto** for reproducible lessons. The sequence below follows the existing draft Master's syllabus; teaching weeks remain subject to the approved calendar.

::: {.callout-tip title="Begin here"}
[Open the first illustrated lesson](../modules/02-data-and-descriptive-statistics/01-data-types-and-toolbox.qmd). Pale lavender title panels, dark text, and restrained Petra accents carry the shared course style into the new lessons. Each lesson combines a business question, a statistical explanation, a visualization, a worked R example, and a short interpretation task.
:::

## Course-to-book mapping

Chapter numbers below refer to this book, not the numbered topics in the syllabus. Read selected sections rather than whole chapters in a single week.

| Week | Course focus | 8th-edition reading | Practical output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | R and RStudio | Instructor introduction; selected context from Chapter 1 | Import data and render a small Quarto report |
| 2 | Data collection, variables, charts | Chapter 1, especially §§1.2–1.5 and 1.9; Chapter 2 §§2.1–2.5 | Data dictionary, frequency tables, appropriate charts |
| 3 | Numerical summaries and probability | Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.5; selected Chapter 4 | Compare groups descriptively; calculate and interpret probabilities |
| 4 | Discrete and continuous distributions | Selected Chapters 5–6 | Compute, simulate, and visualize distributions |
| 5 | Sampling and confidence intervals | Selected Chapters 7–8 | Sampling simulation and intervals for means and proportions |
| 6 | One-sample hypothesis tests | Selected Chapter 9 | Hypotheses, assumptions, confidence interval, p-value, decision |
| 7 | Two-sample comparisons | Selected Chapter 10 | Independent and paired comparisons with uncertainty |
| 8 | ANOVA, chi-square, nonparametric methods | Chapter 13 for ANOVA; Chapter 12 for chi-square; separate notes for rank-based methods | Select a method and justify it; interpret group comparisons |
| 9 | Simple regression | Chapter 14, with R replacing the Excel procedure | Fit, interpret, and diagnose a simple model |
| 10 | Multiple regression | Chapter 15 §§15.1–15.8 | Interpret adjusted effects and categorical predictors |
| 11 | Model building and validation | Chapter 15 for assumptions and diagnostics; separate notes for interactions, selection, and validation | Compare candidate models and evaluate predictions |
| 12 | Time-series forecasting | Supplementary instructor material | Plot trend/seasonality, compare baselines, evaluate holdout error |
| 13 | Business analytics | Chapter 1 §1.7 and selected business cases | Recommendation supported by evidence and limitations |
| 14 | Reproducibility, ethics, future practice | Chapter 1 §1.9 and instructor notes | Reproducible report, provenance, and declared AI use |
| 15 | Integration and review | Selected exercises and cases | Integrated analysis and interpretation practice |

Chapter 11 (population variances) is optional supporting reading when a variance question warrants it. Nonparametric methods, forecasting, and advanced model building need material beyond this volume. The broad syllabus is demanding: use focused examples and scaffolded labs, then revisit concepts in the integrated report.

## Chapters 1–3: teaching sequence

| Lesson | Reading, using printed page numbers | Main question | Visuals and practice |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data and statistical thinking | §§1.2–1.5, pp.5–15; §1.9, pp.22–24 | What does one row represent, and what can the sample tell us? | Original population/sample diagram; restaurant data dictionary |
| Categorical summaries | §2.1, pp.37–46 | Which categories are most common in this sample? | Frequency table, original bar chart, soft-drink label reconciliation |
| Quantitative distributions | §2.2, pp.47–64 | How variable are audit completion times? | Book Figure 2.11, original dot plot and histogram |
| Relationships and chart choices | §§2.3–2.5, pp.65–89 | How do price and rating vary together? | Restaurant crosstab, electronics scatterplot, critique of causal claims |
| Numerical descriptive statistics | §§3.1–3.5, pp.105–152 | What is typical, how much does it vary, and which cases are unusual? | Mean/median comparison, variability, boxplots, and correlation |

Module 2 now teaches these topics through four lessons, their practice, and an integrated review. Introduce only the R functions students need at each step.

## Verified dataset shortlist

The source folder contains **237 Excel files and 200 distinct filenames**. These are inventory counts, not counts of distinct datasets or exact book matches. The old folder's edition label is not used as proof of compatibility.

```{r}
#| label: dataset-shortlist
#| echo: false
# file.exists(): checks whether each specified file path exists.
# read.csv(): reads a comma-separated file into a data frame; its first row supplies column names by default.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
checks_path <- if (file.exists("_instructor/data-checks/dataset-checks.csv")) "_instructor/data-checks/dataset-checks.csv" else "data-checks/dataset-checks.csv"
checks <- read.csv(checks_path)
knitr::kable(checks[c("workbook", "rows", "book_reference", "status")],
  col.names = c("Local file", "Rows", "Book reference", "Verification"))
```

### How these files will be used

- **SoftDrink:** first categorical table/bar-chart example. Preserve the original brands; use a separate mapped-label column for comparison with the book. Matching totals do not establish identical observation order.
- **Audit:** first numeric distribution example. All 20 values match Table 2.4; reuse for location, dispersion, and outliers.
- **Restaurant:** measurement scales, crosstabs, grouped summaries, and later comparisons. Its first 10 displayed rows and all 12 crosstab cells match the book. This is not a row-by-row verification of all 300 records.
- **Stereo:** introductory association example. Its values match the book's **Electronics** example, Table 2.14, despite the different filename. Sales are measured in hundreds of dollars.
- **Butler:** reserve for simple regression. The local file lacks the number-of-deliveries predictor required for the book's multiple-regression example; it is not ready for that lab.

The checked teaching CSVs are in `data/module02/` at the project root. The verification script preserves all source workbooks and fails if an expected comparison changes. [Download the check results](data-checks/dataset-checks.csv) or [view the file inventory](data-checks/inventory.csv).

## Shared lesson and visual design

All new lessons use the same shared stylesheet: pale lavender title panels (**#F5EDF4**), dark title text, a thin Petra accent (**#A83296**), readable white backgrounds, consistent captions, and expandable R code. Section titles provide the visual rhythm of slides while retaining the space needed for explanations and exercises.

For each concept:

1. State the business question and what each observation represents.
2. Explain the statistical idea in plain language.
3. Show a relevant figure and ask students to interpret it.
4. Demonstrate the analysis in R and connect the output to the question.
5. Give a short exercise and an interpretation prompt.

Use selected book figures with the chapter, figure number, printed page, and copyright attribution. The first lesson includes Figure 2.11 (printed p.52). Original charts are generated from checked data in R; conceptual diagrams may be drawn as SVGs or illustrated when useful. Label original and adapted material clearly. Do not imply that a generated illustration is a real observation or that historical teaching data describe today's market.
